papers.title: Circulating gelsolin tracks disease stage in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis across four cohorts
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with highly variable survival, and blood biomarkers beyond neurofilament light chain (NfL) are needed for prognosis and trial stratification. A biomarker of progress through an individualised disease course may be prognostic but independent of the rate of neurodegeneration. We analysed the serum proteome (5,401 proteins) and plasma and cerebrospinal fluid metabolomes (1,659 metabolites) of 94 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and 39 controls recruited in Sheffield, UK, and replicated findings in cohorts from Tel Aviv, Oxford and the United States (AnswerALS). We defined "disease stage" as the fraction of the onset-to-death interval elapsed at sampling. In contrast we define the rate of neurodegeneration by total survival time or the rate of symptom progression quantified using the D50 model of functional decline. Survival-associated proteins were enriched for stage associations in Sheffield (odds ratio = 5.1) and in the Oxford (2.9), and Tel Aviv (1.6) replication cohorts. Sixty-eight proteins not including NfL tracked stage across four cohorts, implicating systemic inflammation and muscle remodelling; the same biology is tracked by 149 plasma and 58 CSF stage-associated metabolites. Stage-associated proteins that rose with stage also rose with age in UK Biobank (17 of 17 age-associated proteins), and the proteomic age gap rose nominally with disease stage (partial Spearman r = 0.25, P = 0.027; BH-adjusted P = 0.055). Circulating gelsolin (GSN) fell with advancing disease in all four cohorts. NfL tracked disease aggressiveness (beta = 0.56, P < 0.001) but not stage (0.13, P = 0.056), whereas GSN tracked stage (-0.41, P <0.001) but not the rate of symptom progression (-0.08, P = 0.25). GSN explained 10% of the variance between patients in disease stage quantified by survival time and 19% of the variance in stage quantified by functional decline; this is comparable to the variance in the rate of neurodegeneration which is captured by circulating NfL. Accounting for disease stage separates markers of disease rate from markers of disease position, refining both biomarker discovery and biological interpretation in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

papers.title: Evaluation of Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) as a biofluid biomarker of cerebral amyloid angiopathy: evidence from neurodegenerative disease and memory clinic cohorts
papers.abstract: Introduction: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is characterised by amyloid-beta (A{beta}) deposition in cerebral vessels, and frequently co-occurs with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diagnosis based on MRI-based Boston criteria is not definitive, and CAA biofluid biomarkers are needed. Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) was recently shown to be selectively enriched in CAA-affected vessels, and correlated with CAA severity. We therefore evaluated SEMA3G as a biofluid biomarker of CAA. Methods: SEMA3G profiles were examined across diagnoses in the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium dataset (GNPC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (N=1982) and plasma (N=6917). SEMA3G was then evaluated in the Healthy Brain Ageing (HBA) memory clinic cohort (N=161) with 3T MRI, where lobar cerebral microbleed burden was used as a proxy for CAA likelihood, with participants grouped by microbleed count (0, 1-2, or [≥]3). Results: CSF and plasma SEMA3G were significantly lower in AD and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) compared to cognitively unimpaired controls in GNPC, and were associated with hypertension. Longitudinally, plasma SEMA3G declined significantly over time in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD. In the HBA cohort, plasma SEMA3G did not differ by cerebral microbleed burden on MRI, nor correlate with plasma A{beta} isoforms and white matter hyperintensities. Discussion: Although CSF and plasma SEMA3G levels were significantly lower in AD and FTD, plasma SEMA3G was not associated with CAA-associated MRI features in individuals at risk of AD. While these findings do not support plasma SEMA3G for identifying individuals with higher CAA-associated burden, its potential utility warrants further evaluation in genetically susceptible or neuropathologically confirmed CAA cohorts.

papers.title: Carotid Artery Stenosis is Associated with Restless Legs Syndrome in the Absence of Stroke
papers.abstract: Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson's disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression. Results: RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005-0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186), indicating a modest but significant association. Conclusion: Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.

papers.title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

papers.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
papers.abstract: Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

papers.title: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and clinical progression in early sporadic Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

papers.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progression is tracked in plasma by systemic proteins independent of motor neurons
papers.abstract: Blood biomarkers that change as patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) decline would allow progression to be monitored more objectively. Plasma proteomic studies have identified proteins that differ between patients and controls, but which plasma proteins change as patients decline, and whether they come from motor neurons, is unknown. Here, we leveraged the Answer ALS cohort, with serial SomaScan plasma proteomics, repeated ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised assessments, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iMNs) from the same patients. At baseline, 77 plasma proteins differed between 245 patients and 76 controls. These were dominated by muscle proteins, including PDLIM3, ACTN2, and MYOM2, and reflected disease severity. Using a two-stage longitudinal design, we identified 72 progression markers whose within-patient change tracked the rate of functional decline, led by CLEC3B, ANTXR2, and ART3. These were largely distinct from the most elevated muscle proteins and were secreted or shed proteins spread across many tissues. Both sets replicated in the independent Target ALS cohort. A motor neuron expression map built from the iMNs showed that motor neuron proteins were underrepresented in both sets and that expression in iMNs did not predict tracking of decline. Baseline serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) predicted how quickly patients declined but its change did not track decline, whereas change in the progression markers did so within every stratum of baseline NfL. Neither tracked decline in the fastest progressing patients. This positions baseline NfL for prognosis and stratification and systemic plasma proteins for monitoring.

papers.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
papers.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

papers.title: ProbeFit: one-seizure qualification and personalisation of multimodal wearable seizure detectors
papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Missed seizures hinder assessment of seizure frequency and treatment. Although wearables can detect seizures automatically, performance varies between patients. Before deployment, it remains difficult to identify suitable patients, and personalisation usually requires several recorded seizures. We propose ProbeFit to predict later seizure sensitivity and personalise a wearable detector from the first recorded seizure. Methods: We used multicentre SeizeIT2 recordings of behind-the-ear EEG, ECG, EMG and movement from 125 patients. Two generic detectors' peak responses to the first seizure generated a qualification probability. The same seizure and preceding background personalised the detector. ProbeFit was developed on 96 patients and applied unchanged to 29 held-out patients. Expert-labelled video-EEG seizures provided the reference. Evaluation compared qualification with the first-seizure heart-rate rule and measured discrimination, calibration and net benefit, and it compared later sensitivity of the generic and personalised detectors at equal false-alarm rates. Results: Among 27 held-out patients with 152 later seizures, qualification correlated with later sensitivity at Spearman {rho} = 0.38, with one-sided p = 0.033. It identified patients with later sensitivity [≥] 0.5 with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.74. Across all 97 evaluable patients, AUC was 0.76 against 0.59 for the heart-rate rule, a difference of 0.17 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.05 to 0.29. At the qualification threshold of 0.5, ProbeFit withheld deployment from 9 of 15 held-out patients below the sensitivity criterion, and its net benefit was 0.074 against -0.111 for selecting everyone. At equal false-alarm rates between 0.25 and 2 per day, personalisation raised later sensitivity by 2.2 percentage points in held-out patients and by 6.3 points in development patients. Both confidence intervals excluded zero, and no held-out patient lost sensitivity. Conclusions: ProbeFit uses the first recorded seizure to predict whether a wearable detector will detect at least half of a patient's later seizures, and it personalises that detector without waiting for further seizures. It supports patient selection and adaptation during the first monitoring admission.

papers.title: Vitamin D Insufficiency and Respiratory Muscle Dysfunction in Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 - A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Introduction: Respiratory complications are a leading cause mortality in myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), making it essential to identify modifiable factors that influence long-term pulmonary function. Vitamin D is known to have an important role in muscle physiology, but its potential relevance for respiratory muscle function has previously not been examined in this patient population. Methods: This was a prospective cohort study including patients with genetically verified DM1 (n = 127) aged 18 years or more. Mean follow-up was 4.3 years. All patients underwent a series of examinations including blood tests and measurement of Vitamin D levels and Forced vital capacity % of predicted (FVC%). Results: Vitamin D insufficiency (<50 nmol/L) was present in 43% of participants. Mean FVC% decreased modestly from 65.7% to 63.6% during follow-up (p=0.004). Patients with vitamin D insufficiency had significantly lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels (54.7% vs 71.2%, p<0.001), and a higher proportion had worsened FVC% (72% vs 50%, p=0.04). In multivariable regression analyses adjusted for disease severity, lower vitamin D levels were independently associated with worse FVC% at follow-up ({beta}=0.12, p=0.04). When vitamin D was examined as a categorical variable in an adjusted model, patients with insufficiency had on average 4.2 percentage points lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels ({beta}=-4.17, p=0.018), independent of baseline lung function and disease severity. Discussion: Lower baseline Vitamin D levels were strongly related to lung function at follow-up in patients with DM1. These findings remained significant after adjusting for potential confounders. However, because FVC% remained largely stable during follow-up, the possibility to assess the long-term effects of vitamin D on change in respiratory function was limited.

papers.title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
papers.abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

papers.title: Imaging and Motor Asymmetry in Parkinson's Disease associated with GBA and LRRK2 mutations: Data from the PPMI study
papers.abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.

papers.title: α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity is associated with motor progression in the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: -Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. Methods: Clinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. Results: We identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. Conclusions: Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.

papers.title: Modifiable and Context-Specific Factors Associated with Dementia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Community-Derived Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

papers.title: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of a Brief Remote Speech Assessment for Screening and Triage of Speech Disorders
papers.abstract: Purpose: Speech abnormalities can often be early or clinically important manifestations of neurologic disease, yet access to clinicians with specialized expertise required for comprehensive motor speech evaluation may limit timely assessment. Brief remote speech assessment could provide a scalable approach for identifying patients who warrant more comprehensive evaluation, but its utility across heterogeneous speech presentations remains unclear. This study evaluated the validity and clinical utility of the Mayo Speech Test (MST), a brief (~5-minute) audio-recorded remote speech assessment, relative to a comprehensive in-person motor speech examination (~1-hour). Specifically, we examined whether MST could support clinically meaningful screening and triage decisions by distinguishing normal from abnormal speech and identifying the presence of a speech disorder. Method: One hundred participants completed a comprehensive in-person speech evaluation and a remote MST. Participants were excluded when the interval between assessments exceeded 90 days (n = 13) or either rater judged audio quality insufficient for diagnostic interpretation (n = 6), with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final analytic sample of 82 participants. Remote recordings were independently evaluated by two speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who were blinded to participant identity. In-person evaluation classifications served as the clinical reference standard and were grouped as normal (n = 33), dysphonia only (n = 5), or speech disorder (n = 43). One participant could not be classified. Performance was evaluated for two clinically motivated binary decisions: distinguishing normal from abnormal (such as dysphonia or speech disorder; Tier 0) and identifying normal speech or dysphonia only versus speech disorder (Tier 1). Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, agreement, and error patterns were examined. Results: Both remote raters demonstrated similar overall performance despite differing error profiles. For Tier 0 screening, Rater 1 demonstrated 93.6% sensitivity and 71.9% specificity for identifying abnormal voice/speech, whereas Rater 2 demonstrated 78.7% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity. For Tier 1 identification of speech disorder, sensitivity and specificity were 83.3% and 86.5%, respectively, for Rater 1 and 71.4% and 97.4% for Rater 2. Interrater agreement was 79.7% for Tier 0 ({kappa} = 0.60) and 86.1% for Tier 1 ({kappa} = 0.72). Missed speech disorders represented an important source of error, with differences between raters indicating distinct thresholds for assigning abnormality and speech-disorder classifications. Conclusions: A brief remote speech assessment showed promising performance for broad clinical classification, particularly when used to address screening and triage questions rather than reproduce the diagnostic granularity of a comprehensive examination. Similar overall performance across raters masked meaningful sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs, highlighting the importance of examining error profiles in addition to aggregate accuracy. MST may therefore have clinical utility for identifying patients who warrant comprehensive motor speech evaluation, but should not be considered a substitute for a full diagnostic assessment.

papers.title: Adverse Events and Baseline Psychological Distress Among Dementia Family Care Partners in the Tele-STELLA Study
papers.abstract: Background: Adverse event (AE) narratives may reveal physical and psychological challenges experienced by family care partners of people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Objective: To characterize care partner AEs during the national Tele-STELLA study and explore differences in baseline psychological characteristics by AE category and subcategory. Methods: This descriptive, exploratory analysis included 43 AEs reported by 36 care partners. Narratives were classified as Physical, Psychological, or Random/Other. Baseline depressive symptoms, grief, and behavioral reactivity were compared between care partners with and without each AE type within this sample. Results: Physcial events accounted for 48.8% of AEs, Psychological events for 39.5%, and Random/Other events for 11.6%. Infections predominated among Physical events; stress/distress accounted for half of the Psychological events. Psychological AEs were associated with higher baseline grief and behavioral reactivity. Stress/distress-related AEs were associated with higher depressive symptoms and reactivity, whereas aggression-related Aes were associated with greater grief. Conclusions: Care partner AE narratives captured heterogeneous physical and psychological experiences. Classification may complement conventional assessments of care partner health and distress. These exploratory findings do not establish causality or predictive validity and warrant prospective study.

papers.title: Central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation at 5 Hz or 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation for ataxia in multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type: a retrospective cohort study of efficacy and predictors of response
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) at different frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz) combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation on the core domains of ataxia in patients with multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C), and to explore the independent predictors of the response. Methods: In this retrospective study, 48 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of MSA-C were included. All patients received bilateral cerebellar hemispheric 1 Hz rTMS as background therapy and were divided according to the frequency of central cortical stimulation into a control group (cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation only, n=15), a 5 Hz combination group (n=16) and a 10 Hz combination group (n=17). Ataxia severity before and after treatment was assessed with the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS); absolute improvements and improvement rates were calculated for each subscore and for the total score. Continuous variables were described as mean +/- standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) according to normality; within-group pre-post comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group comparisons used one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction. Clinical response was defined by an absolute improvement threshold (delta-ICARS total score >= 8 points), and independent influencing factors were analysed by Firth-penalised logistic regression; sensitivity analyses were performed with a total-score improvement rate >= 20% (and with >= 15% and >= 30% as alternative thresholds), and robustness results are reported for the delta-ICARS >= 10-point criterion. Missing cognitive and mood scale scores were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5; the mean of the five imputations constituted the analysis dataset) and then included in the analysis. Subgroup and interaction analyses were performed according to the median disease duration (2 years) and median age (57 years). Results: After treatment, the ICARS total score in the overall cohort was significantly lower than at baseline (median difference 7.0 points, P = 20% was used to define clinically significant efficacy, the response rates of the three groups were 6.7%, 50.0% and 58.8% (P=0.006), and both the 10 Hz and 5 Hz groups were significantly better than the control group (Bonferroni-corrected P=0.006 and P=0.040), with no statistically significant difference between the two frequencies. Domain-specific comparison showed statistically significant between-group differences in both the absolute improvement and the improvement rate of limb kinetic function (P=0.013 and P=0.005), with the 10 Hz group significantly better than the control group. When clinical response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 8 points, the response rates of the three groups were 20.0%, 56.2% and 64.7% (P=0.029); Firth-penalised multivariable regression showed that baseline ICARS total score was an independent predictor of clinical response (OR=1.076, 95% CI 1.013-1.143, P=0.017), whereas 5 Hz (OR=4.298, 95% CI 0.757-24.412, P=0.100) and 10 Hz (OR=5.847, 95% CI 0.885-38.640, P=0.067) stimulation did not reach independent statistical significance after adjustment. When response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 10 points, the response rates were 0%, 43.8% and 47.1% (P=0.007), and there were no responders in the control group. Subgroup analysis showed a significant group-by-age interaction (P=0.020); the clinical response rate of patients aged >= 57 years receiving 10 Hz stimulation was 85.7% (exploratory finding; small subgroup sample). The group-by-duration interaction was not statistically significant (P=0.210). Conclusions: Central 5 Hz and 10 Hz rTMS combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation both significantly improved the symptoms of ataxia in patients with MSA-C, and the efficacy was domain-specific, with the greatest improvement in the limb kinetic domain; sensitivity analyses across multiple criteria (delta-ICARS >= 8 points, improvement rate >= 20%, delta-ICARS >= 10 points) consistently supported the efficacy benefit of high-frequency stimulation in the same direction, but stimulation frequency did not reach independent predictive statistical significance after adjustment, and baseline ICARS total score was significantly associated with absolute improvement. Age may have a modifying effect on the efficacy of stimulation frequency (exploratory finding; small sample). This study provides preliminary support for the efficacy of the central 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz regimen; the optimal stimulation parameters and independent predictors remain to be verified in larger prospective studies.

papers.title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT =5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI =5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI =5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

papers.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
papers.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

papers.title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
papers.abstract: Background and ObjectivesNormative modeling expresses an individuals brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. MethodsWe retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). ResultsWe included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. DiscussionUnivariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomic Identifies GDF15 as a Candidate Lithium Treatment Response Biomarker in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Secondary Analysis of the LATTICE Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Lithium (Li) demonstrates neuroprotective effects relevant to Alzheimers disease (AD); however, its molecular mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study analyzed plasma proteomic profiles from the Li as a Treatment to Prevent Impairment of Cognition in Elders (LATTICE) randomized clinical trial to identify markers associated with amyloid (A{beta}) pathology, disease progression, and response to Li treatment. In the LATTICE trial, 80 older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were randomly assigned to receive either low-dose Li carbonate or placebo for two years. Longitudinal plasma samples were analyzed using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120 proteomic panel. Baseline protein levels were compared according to randomized treatment assignment, A{beta}-PET status, and MCI subtype. Analyses included longitudinal changes in protein levels associated with treatment and time, associations between baseline protein levels and subsequent cognitive, functional, and neuroimaging trajectories, and the influence of baseline protein levels on Li treatment effects. Among the 80 participants, 62 had amnestic MCI and 21 were A{beta}-PET positive. Baseline proteomic differences were more strongly associated with A{beta}-PET status than with randomized treatment assignment. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations were elevated in A{beta}-PET positive individuals and remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Over time, CALB2 and TREM2 exhibited nominal treatment-by-time interactions in the full cohort, while in the amnestic MCI subgroup, CALB2, TREM2, and A{beta}40 demonstrated nominal effects; none persisted after multiple-testing correction. GDF15 showed the most consistent associations with CDR Sum of Boxes trajectories and treatment-effect modification that remained significant after false discovery rate correction in the amnestic MCI subgroup, whereas p-tau217 was most consistently associated with hippocampal volume trajectories. Other protein-outcome associations were exploratory. Plasma proteomics identified distinct molecular patterns associated with A{beta} pathology and the MCI phenotype, along with exploratory evidence of Li-associated protein changes. Plasma GDF15 and p-tau217 emerged as potential markers of clinical progression and treatment-response heterogeneity, warranting validation in larger, adequately powered trials.

papers.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
papers.abstract: ObjectiveClear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. MethodsWe used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinsons disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. ResultsCombined saccade-vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade-assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7-49.3%; p{approx}0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. ConclusionsThese findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. SignificanceBinocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

papers.title: Circulating Apolipoprotein Profiles and Their Associations with Mild Cognitive and Behavioral Impairment in Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild behavioral impairment (MBI) are overlapping prodromal states associated with dementia risk. Circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) may be linked to cognitive and behavioral changes, but their relationships remain unclear. ObjectiveExamine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos in prodromal dementia. MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 148 Thai participants aged 60-75 years: 56 cognitively normal controls, 47 with MCI without MBI, and 45 with MBI with or without MCI. We measured ApoA1, ApoA2, ApoB, ApoC1, ApoC3, ApoD, ApoE, ApoH, and ApoJ, five lipids, and APOE genotype, and computed an atherogenic Apo composite (ApoB-ApoC1-ApoC3). Primary analyses used multivariable linear regression of quantitative cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Group comparisons were secondary and served to contextualize the dimensional regression findings. ResultsAcross Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) models, 20.7-28.2% of variance was explained by combinations of ApoH, ApoC3, APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status, age, and male sex (inverse associations), and free cholesterol and education (positive associations). The atherogenic composite was inversely associated with MoCA total, memory index, and delayed recall scores, and with Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimers Disease (CERAD) verbal fluency and word list recall. No significant predictors emerged for Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) scores or NPI caregiver distress. All nine Apos differed significantly between groups, with levels highest in MCI, intermediate in MBI, and lowest in controls. ConclusionsCirculating Apo profiles differed across controls, MCI, and MBI groups and were more consistently associated with cognitive than behavioral outcomes. ApoH and the atherogenic Apo composite warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of early cognitive dysfunction.

papers.title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
papers.abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center, Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

papers.title: Greater medial temporal lobe atrophy is associated with less severe cardiac sympathetic denervation in dementia with Lewy bodies
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiac sympathetic denervation varies in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Our previous neuropathological study demonstrated an association between greater Alzheimers disease (AD) pathology and milder cardiac sympathetic denervation in DLB. We investigated whether medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA), a potential marker of concomitant AD pathology, correlates with cardiac sympathetic denervation assessed by 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy in probable DLB. MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed 162 patients with probable DLB. MTA was assessed by VSRAD Z-scores, and cardiac MIBG uptake by early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios. Associations were examined using Spearman and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and disease duration. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with MIBG-dependent classification, diabetes mellitus or cardiac disease. ResultsVSRAD Z-scores correlated positively with early ({rho} = 0.173, P = 0.028) and delayed H/M ratios ({rho} = 0.225, P = 0.004). After adjustment, the association was no longer significant for the early H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.133, P = 0.094), whereas it remained significant for the delayed H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.196, P = 0.013). The adjusted delayed H/M association persisted after excluding 18 patients with MIBG-dependent classification ({rho} = 0.211, P = 0.012) and 40 with diabetes or cardiac disease ({rho} = 0.231, P = 0.011). ConclusionsGreater MTA was associated with relatively preserved cardiac MIBG uptake in probable DLB, particularly on delayed imaging. Consistent with our neuropathological observations, these findings suggest that concomitant AD pathology may contribute to variability in cardiac sympathetic denervation.

papers.title: Inter-articulatory Timing of Vocalic Tongue Body and Jaw Movements across Talkers with Dysarthria due to Various Neurological Conditions
papers.abstract: PurposeThis study compared inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and jaw across talkers with Parkinsons disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntingtons disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurotypical controls (CON) to identify disease-related differences. The study also explored if a talkers tongue body cycle duration, which serve as a proxy for a talkers habitual speech rate, or a talkers reliance on their jaw, as indicated by their jaw movement amplitude, could predict their inter-articulatory timing patterns. MethodUsing three-dimensional electromagnetic articulography, the movements of the posterior tongue and jaw were examined in 24 talkers with PD, 19 talkers with ALS, 18 talkers with HD, 18 talkers with MS, and 34 CON during a sentence repetition task ("Buy Kaia a kite"). The tongue movement during the segment [kai] served as the reference signal (tongue body cycle) for which the phase angle of the jaw reaching the maximum opening position during [kai] was calculated. Tongue body cycle durations were measured as the time between the tongue body movement onset to the tongue body movement offset. The jaw opening amplitude was measured as the relative positional change from the jaws maximum closing position associated with [k] to the jaws maximal opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai]. ResultsA significant group effect was found for phase angles. Pairwise comparisons showed that talkers with ALS had significantly larger phase angles than talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON, indicating a timing pattern where the tongue reached the target [a] earlier relative to the jaw. No significant differences were found for any other pairwise comparisons. Furthermore, no significant associations were found between tongue body cycle durations and phase angles. A significant association was found between jaw amplitudes and phase angles when considering all talkers [rS(110) = .253, p = .008] and when only considering talkers of the control group [r(34) = .361, p = .036]. ConclusionsFindings suggest that during the production of [kai], tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS differ from those of talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON with the tongue reaching the maximum opening position before the jaw while the opposite pattern was observed for talkers of the other groups. However, the variability in tongue body cycle duration did not significantly contribute to the variability in phase angles and the variability in jaw amplitudes only accounted for 6% of the variability in phase angles across all talkers. Future studies are needed to determine if the observed tongue-jaw timing pattern of talkers with ALS generalizes to other phonetic contexts and determine the underlying factors that contribute to the unique tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS.

papers.title: Timing of First Poststroke Seizure and Risk of Seizure Recurrence by Stroke Subtype
papers.abstract: ImportanceThe 7-day cutoff separating acute symptomatic from unprovoked poststroke seizures guides epilepsy diagnosis and long-term antiseizure medication but is consensus based and unvalidated against recurrence risk by stroke subtype. ObjectiveTo determine whether seizure recurrence risk changes abruptly at day 7 and how it varies with first-seizure timing by stroke subtype. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsThis pooled analysis of individual participant data from 36 cohorts in 22 countries (inclusion, 1994-2025) included adults with a first seizure after ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, or cerebral venous thrombosis. ExposureDays from stroke onset (or venous thrombosis diagnosis) to first seizure. Main Outcomes and MeasuresThe 10-year cumulative incidence of unprovoked seizure recurrence, with death as a competing event, from stabilized inverse probability of treatment- weighted Fine-Gray spline models. Risk zones were based on the likelihood of being helped vs harmed and the 60% epilepsy threshold of the International League Against Epilepsy. ResultsOf 2434 individuals (median [IQR] age, 63 [49-75] years; 1181 [48.5%] female), 684 (28.1%) had a seizure recurrence. Risk changed gradually with first-seizure timing, without a day-7 transition; overall 10-year risk differed by subtype (cerebral venous thrombosis, 44%; intracerebral hemorrhage, 43%; ischemic stroke, 40%; subarachnoid hemorrhage, 35%; P < .001). At day 7, the 10-year risk was 24% (95% CI, 17%-32%) after ischemic stroke, 30% (95% CI, 22%-38%) after intracerebral hemorrhage, 41% (95% CI, 22%-53%) after subarachnoid hemorrhage, and 58% (95% CI, 44%-71%) after cerebral venous thrombosis. The 60% threshold was crossed from day 71 after ischemic stroke, day 41 after intracerebral hemorrhage, and day 9 after cerebral venous thrombosis; after subarachnoid hemorrhage, only seizures on days 2 to 3 exceeded it. Mortality was inversely related to recurrence risk. Of 800 first seizures after day 7 following ischemic stroke or intracerebral hemorrhage, which would qualify as epilepsy under current criteria, 335 (42%) had a recurrence risk below the 60% diagnostic threshold. Conclusions and RelevanceIn this pooled analysis, seizure recurrence risk after stroke rose gradually, not abruptly at day 7, and differed by subtype. After external validation, subtype-specific risk zones could inform individualized decisions about long-term antiseizure medication. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDoes seizure recurrence risk change abruptly at day 7, the boundary separating acute symptomatic from unprovoked seizures after stroke? FindingsIn this pooled analysis of individual participant data from 2434 adults with poststroke seizures, 10-year seizure recurrence risk rose gradually with first-seizure timing, without a day-7 step, and differed by stroke subtype; the 60% epilepsy threshold was reached from day 71 after ischemic stroke, day 41 after intracerebral hemorrhage, and day 9 after cerebral venous thrombosis. MeaningA single 7-day cutoff does not reflect seizure recurrence risk after stroke; subtype-specific risk zones may better guide long-term antiseizure medication decisions.

papers.title: Loneliness is associated with 15-year risk of stroke: The Framingham Heart Study
papers.abstract: Psychosocial factors are promising candidates as modifiable risk factors for stroke. Loneliness is of interest given its rising prevalence worldwide; yet the temporal relationship of loneliness with subsequent stroke remains unclear. AimTo clarify the association between timing of loneliness and incident stroke. MethodsFramingham Heart Study participants free of stroke with at least two assessments of loneliness prior to incident stroke (at baseline exam, and at prior exam up to 15 years before baseline) were included. Loneliness was assessed using response to the "I felt lonely" item on the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, defined as feeling lonely for [≥]3 days within the past week. The recency of loneliness was defined as prior loneliness (present at the prior exam) and baseline loneliness (present at the baseline exam). The primary analysis tested separately for associations between prior loneliness vs no prior loneliness, baseline versus no baseline loneliness, and incident stroke, with 15 years of follow up. Cox models were adjusted for age and sex (model 1) and additionally vascular risk factors (model 2), depressive symptoms (model 3), and physical activity (model 4). Interactions between loneliness and age and sex were explored. ResultAmong 4307 participants (mean age 62{+/-}10 years, 55% women), 198 (4.5%) had an incident stroke over a median 6.5-year follow-up period. Prior loneliness was reported by 177 (4.1%) and 226 (5.2%) reported baseline loneliness. Compared to participants without prior loneliness, those with prior loneliness had nearly 3-fold increase in stroke risk after adjustment for age, sex, vascular risk factors, depressive symptoms, and physical activity (HR=2.85, 95% [CI] 1.51-5.39). The effect was primarily observed in participants <80 years (mean age 60 years.HR=3.21, 95% CI 1.69-6.13). No increased risk of stroke was observed among participants with loneliness at baseline. ConclusionOur findings support consideration of loneliness as a potentially modifiable risk factor, particularly in midlife, for incident stroke. 3-5 Bullet pointsO_LILoneliness, reported on average 7.6 years prior to a baseline exam, was associated with long-term risk of incident stroke C_LIO_LIThe increased risk of stroke associated with prior loneliness was observed independent of vascular risk factors, the presence of depressive symptoms, or physical activity status C_LIO_LIThe association between prior loneliness and incident stroke was observed primarily in individuals <80 years, around a mean age of 60 years, representing an independent risk factor that may be present at mid-life C_LIO_LIEfforts to address loneliness, early in the life course, may reduce future stroke incidence C_LI

papers.title: In-country cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next generation sequencing for pathogen detection in Lima, Peru
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe epidemiology of central nervous system (CNS) infections in low- and middle-income countries is poorly characterized due to limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) can detect any pathogen in a single hypothesis-free assay but has largely been confined to high-income countries due to cost and infrastructure requirements. We piloted an in-country CSF mNGS protocol in Lima, Peru to assess the feasibility of this approach in a resource-limited setting. MethodsAdults with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo were enrolled. CSF mNGS (DNA and RNA) was performed in-country on a benchtop sequencer with half-volume library reactions and cloud-based analysis (CZID). Paired sequencing at a significantly higher depth was performed on a subset of samples in the United States for validation. ResultsAmong 43 participants (median age 48 years; 21% living with HIV), in-country mNGS detected 20 pathogens in 18 samples (42%), of which 65% were not identified by routine clinical testing. Nine of 15 patients treated empirically for tuberculous meningitis were found to have a non-mycobacterial infection. Detected organisms included Toxoplasma gondii, Taenia solium, Treponema pallidum, herpesviruses, and, on deeper sequencing, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus. Deep sequencing recovered four pathogens missed at shallower-depth. ConclusionsIn-country CSF mNGS was feasible in Lima, Peru and recovered a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens, most missed by routine testing. By utilizing available, lower-output sequencers, we overcame a principal barrier to deploying this technology where the burden of undiagnosed CNS infection is greatest.
